newsitem.title: HONGKONG: Handover venue adds new glow to Hong Kong waterfront.
newsitem.headline: Handover venue adds new glow to Hong Kong waterfront.

text.p: The ceremonial venue for Hong Kong's historic handover to Chinese rule won its race against time by officially opening on Saturday -- but with a few leaks in the roof still to be plugged.

The just-completed extension of the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre glowed on the waterfront like a giant electric turtle after the territory's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, officially lit up the huge structure jutting into the harbour.

The opening ended weeks of suspense over whether the building, where Britian's Prince Charles and China's President Jiang Zemin would preside over the ceremony marking Hong Kong's handover at midnight of June 30, would be finished in time.

The striking, HK$4.8 billion (US$615 million) building shot up in just 39 months on a man-made island on the Wanchai waterfront -- once known only for its girlie bars but now also home to many gleaming office towers and top-notch hotels.

"It is a vision of Hong Kong as Asia's pre-eminent city in international business," said Victor Fung, chairman of Hong Kong's Trade Development Council (TDC), describing the building's wing-shaped roof.
"It is much more than just a pretty face on the Wanchai waterfront," he said.
But even Tung, who will be sworn in as Chief Executive of the territory of 6.4 million people before dawn on July 1 after the handover ceremony, confessed he had had his doubts.

"Victor," he said in a speech at a charity gala inaugurating the building. "That time in January when you brought me into this very room and I saw all those sacks of cement, even I began to wonder whether TDC would finish it on time."
Up until last month bamboo scaffolding -- the remnants of 450 kilometres (280 miles) of bamboo used in the project -- still covered much of the glass facade overlooking the harbour.
But the project was finished, aside from some cleaning and internal fitting out, Niels Kraunsoe, the centre's chief executive, told reporters.

Although the building was declared completed, officials were facing some leaks in the gigantic roof. But they promised to keep the VIP guests from 40 countries dry on the night that Britain hands Hong Kong over to Beijing.

Journalists given a sneak preview saw water dripping from the ceiling of the Grand Hall of the centre on Friday and Saturday after torrential rains fell on Hong Kong as workmen hurried to put finishing touches on the ceremonial venue.
Kraunsoe said the leak was sheer bad luck as rain happened to bucket down as workmen serviced the 200 pipes that drain the four hectare (10 acre) roof.
He swore the problem was now fixed, although journalists saw water still dripping in some parts of the building only hours before the inagural banquet got under way.
"There's no contingency plan, it's not going to drip on the night, it's not going to drip tomorrow," he promised.
The handover ceremony will take place on a specially constructed stage -- whose top-secret design is still veiled from sight -- in a Grand Foyer, with the harbour as backdrop.
The guests will be sitting in the Grand Hall, which normally faces the other way but whose seating arrangement was turned north toward the stage -- and Beijing -- for the ceremony.
Following the handover ceremony, almost everybody will walk to one of the exhibit halls where the new Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government will be sworn in.

Kraunsoe said moving 4,000 or so people could take up to 45 minutes -- ample time for those boycotting the inauguration of a controversial provisional legislature, such as U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and British Prime Minister Tony Blair, to duck out.
